warmup.q: A ledger holds 50 accounts with 500,000 cents in total. Eight threads make 100,000 random transfers each with if (balance[from] >= c) { balance[from] -= c; balance[to] += c; } on a plain long[], with no locks. What is the total at the end?
options: Exactly 500,000, because every transfer adds what it subtracts
Some other number, different on every run
Exactly 500,000, but some balances are negative
warmup.why: Each -= and += is a read, a change and a write. When two threads update the same account at the same moment, one of the two updates is lost. A lost debit creates money and a lost credit destroys it, so the total drifts, by millions of cents in the demo below. Nothing throws: a plain array has no checks at all.

sections.h: Write the invariants down before the code
sections.html:
Here is the smallest ledger that can be wrong. Fifty accounts, no locks:

Java
long[] balance = new long[50];          // 10,000 cents each, 500,000 in total

void transfer(int from, int to, long cents) {
    if (balance[from] >= cents) {       // check
        balance[from] -= cents;         // read, subtract, write
        balance[to] += cents;           // read, add, write
    }
}
Kotlin
val balance = LongArray(50) { 10_000L } // 500,000 cents in total

fun transfer(from: Int, to: Int, cents: Long) {
    if (balance[from] >= cents) {       // check
        balance[from] -= cents          // read, subtract, write
        balance[to] += cents            // read, add, write
    }
}

Run it on eight threads with 100,000 random transfers each, and the total is wrong by millions of cents. You know the mechanism from Race conditions: why count++ lies: -= is a read, a subtraction and a write, and two threads that read the same balance lose one of the two updates.

Before you write the real ledger, write down what correct means. An invariant is a statement about the data that must be true whenever another thread can look. This ledger has three:

  1. Money is conserved: the sum of all balances never changes.
  2. No balance is ever below zero.
  3. A transfer happens whole or not at all: nobody sees the debit without the credit.

Each invariant decides part of the design. Invariants 1 and 3 say the debit and the credit must be one step that no other thread can split, and that step spans two accounts. Invariant 2 says the balance check belongs inside that same step. A check in one step and a debit in another is check-then-act, the second race shape from that lesson. And "whenever another thread can look" tells you where to test: not only at the end of a run.

The rest of this lesson builds the ledger so that every line of apply points at one of these three. That is the habit to keep for any shared state: invariants first, then the locks that protect them, then a test that tries hard to break them.

try.title: Count what a lock-free ledger loses
steps: Open BrokenLedgerDemo (or its Kotlin twin). Before you run it, write down what you expect the total to be after each run.
Run it with the command below. Note how far off each run is.
Run it again with -Pargs=1000, so each thread makes only 1,000 transfers. The threads still start behind a latch. Predict first: will the total be right?

code.title: BrokenLedgerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; /** A ledger with no locks: 8 threads move money between 50 accounts. Count what goes wrong. */ public class BrokenLedgerDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final long OPENING = 10_000; // cents per account: 500,000 in total public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 100_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { long[] balance = new long[ACCOUNTS]; Arrays.fill(balance, OPENING); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread w = new Thread(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) { int from = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS), to = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS); if (from == to) continue; long cents = 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000); if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents; // act: read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents; // read, add, write } } }); w.start(); workers.add(w); } go.countDown(); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); long total = 0; for (long b : balance) total += b; System.out.printf("run %d: total %,d cents, expected 500,000, off by %,d%n", run, total, total - ACCOUNTS * OPENING); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread private const val ACCOUNTS = 50 private const val OPENING = 10_000L // cents per account: 500,000 in total /** A ledger with no locks: 8 threads move money between 50 accounts. Count what goes wrong. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 100_000 for (run in 1..3) { val balance = LongArray(ACCOUNTS) { OPENING } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(8) { thread { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() go.await() repeat(perThread) { val from = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS) val to = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS) if (from != to) { val cents = 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000) if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents // act: read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents // read, add, write } } } } } go.countDown() workers.forEach { it.join() } val total = balance.sum() println("run %d: total %,d cents, expected 500,000, off by %,d".format(run, total, total - ACCOUNTS * OPENING)) } }

try.expect: With 100,000 transfers per thread the total is off by millions of cents, and by a different amount every run (one run here ended at 5,222,671 cents instead of 500,000). With 1,000 per thread it is still wrong, by thousands: the latch releases all eight threads at the same moment, so even short runs collide. Without the latch, short runs often look correct because each thread finishes before the next one starts.

sections.h: A transfer is a value, so make it immutable
sections.html:
A transfer crosses threads. An HTTP handler or a file importer builds it, a pool thread applies it, the journal writes it and a log line prints it. If any of them can change it, the others can see two versions of it.

Here is that bug in its most common form. A batch importer parses a file into one reusable row object, to save allocations, and hands each row to a pool:

Java
TransferRow row = new TransferRow();             // mutable, reused for every line
for (String line : file) {
    row.parse(line);                             // overwrites id, from, to, cents
    pool.execute(() -> ledger.apply(row));       // a worker reads row later
}
Kotlin
val row = TransferRow()                          // mutable, reused for every line
for (line in file) {
    row.parse(line)                              // overwrites id, from, to, cents
    pool.execute { ledger.apply(row) }           // a worker reads row later
}

By the time a worker reads row, the parser has moved on. In this section's demo, 100,000 lines reached the ledger as about 11,000 different transfers, most of them applied several times. A few dozen rows carried the id of one line and the amount of another. That is a data race: the worker read the fields with no happens-before edge to the parser's later writes, so it could see any mix of them.

The fix is a value that can't change. A Java record, or a Kotlin data class of vals, has final fields and no setters:

Java
public record Transfer(String id, String from, String to, long cents) {
    public Transfer {                            // compact constructor: runs before the fields are set
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
        Objects.requireNonNull(from, "from");
        Objects.requireNonNull(to, "to");
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        if (from.equals(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("two different accounts");
    }
}
Kotlin
data class Transfer(val id: String, val from: String, val to: String, val cents: Long) {
    init {                                       // runs on every construction, copy() included
        require(cents > 0) { "amount must be positive" }
        require(from != to) { "two different accounts" }
    }
}

Two things come with it. As Safe publication, final fields and escaping this showed, an object with only final fields that doesn't leak this is seen whole by any thread, however it gets there. And the checks run once, at construction, so a Transfer that exists is valid. The ledger never asks whether cents is negative or from equals to, and the lock-ordering code in the next section relies on two different accounts.

Money is a long of cents. A double can't hold 0.10 exactly, and a ledger that drifts by fractions of a cent breaks invariant 1 with no thread involved.

try.title: Reuse one row, then use a record
steps: Run ReusedTransferDemo. It parses 100,000 lines and hands each one to a pool of 4 threads. Predict first: how many different lines reach the ledger?
Run it again with -Pargs=record, which builds a new immutable Transfer for each line.

code.title: ReusedTransferDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** An importer parses 100,000 lines and hands each one to a pool. Pass "record" to use an immutable value. */ public class ReusedTransferDemo { // the mutable row a parser fills in for each line, then reuses for the next line static final class TransferRow { String id; long cents; } record Transfer(String id, long cents) {} // immutable: one new value per line public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean immutable = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("record"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); LongAdder appliedCents = new LongAdder(); Set<String> appliedLines = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); AtomicInteger mixed = new AtomicInteger(); long fileCents = 0; TransferRow row = new TransferRow(); for (int line = 0; line < 100_000; line++) { long cents = 100 + line % 900; fileCents += cents; if (immutable) { Transfer t = new Transfer("line-" + line, cents); pool.execute(() -> applyLine(t.id(), t.cents(), appliedCents, appliedLines, mixed)); } else { row.id = "line-" + line; // overwrite the shared row... row.cents = cents; pool.execute(() -> applyLine(row.id, row.cents, appliedCents, appliedLines, mixed)); // ...read it later } } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("file: 100,000 lines, %,d cents%n", fileCents); System.out.printf("applied: %,d different lines, %,d cents, %,d rows mixing two lines%n", appliedLines.size(), appliedCents.sum(), mixed.get()); } // stands in for ledger.apply: records what the worker saw static void applyLine(String id, long cents, LongAdder appliedCents, Set<String> lines, AtomicInteger mixed) { appliedCents.add(cents); lines.add(id); int line = Integer.parseInt(id.substring("line-".length())); if (cents != 100 + line % 900) mixed.incrementAndGet(); // the id and the amount came from different lines } }

alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder // the mutable row a parser fills in for each line, then reuses for the next line private class ImportRow { var id = "" var cents = 0L } private data class ImportedTransfer(val id: String, val cents: Long) // immutable: one new value per line private val appliedCents = LongAdder() private val appliedLines: MutableSet<String> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() private val mixed = AtomicInteger() /** An importer parses 100,000 lines and hands each one to a pool. Pass "record" to use an immutable value. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val immutable = args.firstOrNull() == "record" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) var fileCents = 0L val row = ImportRow() for (line in 0 until 100_000) { val cents = 100L + line % 900 fileCents += cents if (immutable) { val t = ImportedTransfer("line-$line", cents) pool.execute { applyLine(t.id, t.cents) } } else { row.id = "line-$line" // overwrite the shared row... row.cents = cents pool.execute { applyLine(row.id, row.cents) } // ...read it later } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("file: 100,000 lines, %,d cents".format(fileCents)) println("applied: %,d different lines, %,d cents, %,d rows mixing two lines".format(appliedLines.size, appliedCents.sum(), mixed.get())) } // stands in for ledger.apply: records what the worker saw private fun applyLine(id: String, cents: Long) { appliedCents.add(cents) appliedLines += id val line = id.removePrefix("line-").toInt() if (cents != 100L + line % 900) mixed.incrementAndGet() // the id and the amount came from different lines }

try.expect: With the reused row only a fraction of the lines arrive (between 10,000 and 13,000 in runs here), the cents don't add up, and a few dozen rows mix one line's id with another line's amount. With a record all 100,000 lines arrive, the totals match and nothing is mixed. Each record is built once, handed to the pool (an executor hand-off is a happens-before edge), and never written again.

sections.h: Per-account locks, taken in one global order
sections.html:
Invariants 1 and 3 need the debit and the credit to happen as one step. The simplest way is one lock for the whole ledger. It is correct, and it makes two transfers that share no account wait for each other. With one lock per account, a transfer between accounts 3 and 7 and another between 12 and 40 can run at the same time.

Per-account locks bring back the bug from Deadlock, livelock and starvation: a transfer from A to B locks A and waits for B, while a transfer from B to A holds B and waits for A. The fix from that lesson applies as it is. Give every account a unique, stable key and always lock the smaller key first:

Java
public Outcome apply(Transfer t) {
    Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to());
    Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to;   // 1. one order for everyone
    Account second = first == from ? to : from;
    first.lock().lock();
    try {
        second.lock().lock();
        try {
            if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS;   // 2. check...
            from.debit(t.cents());                                         // 3. ...and act
            to.credit(t.cents());
            return Outcome.APPLIED;
        } finally {
            second.lock().unlock();
        }
    } finally {
        first.lock().unlock();                                             // 4. on every path
    }
}
Kotlin
fun apply(t: Transfer): Outcome {
    val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to)
    val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to                      // 1. one order for everyone
    val second = if (first === from) to else from
    return first.lock.withLock {
        second.lock.withLock {
            if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS  // 2. check...
            from.debit(t.cents)                                            // 3. ...and act
            to.credit(t.cents)
            Outcome.APPLIED
        }
    }                                                                      // 4. withLock unlocks in finally
}

Each line traces back to an invariant. The order (1) removes the cycle that a deadlock needs. The check sits under both locks (2), so no other transfer can spend the same money between the check and the debit. Debit and credit share one critical section (3), so a thread that takes these locks never sees half a transfer. And finally (4) releases both locks on every path, including the early return for a refusal.

The account id is a String compared with compareTo. It is unique and never changes, and that is all an order needs. hashCode() would not do: two accounts can share a hash code, and then two threads can disagree about which one comes first.

Why ReentrantLock and not synchronized? Here they behave the same. The choice pays off in lesson 3 of this track: on JDK 21, a virtual thread waiting to enter a synchronized block holds on to its carrier thread, and a ledger serving 10,000 virtual threads will have waiters.

What do per-account locks buy? Run the demo and count. With one lock, at most one transfer is ever in progress. With per-account locks, about as many as you have cores. Whether that also makes it faster depends on how much work sits inside the lock and on what else your machine is doing, so the demo prints both.

try.title: Count the transfers in progress
steps: Run LockGranularityDemo. It runs the same 400,000 random transfers under one ledger-wide lock, then under per-account locks taken in id order. Each transfer does 50 steps of work inside its lock.
Before you read the output, predict the last column, "most transfers in progress at once", for each strategy.
Run it with -Pargs=0 (no work inside the lock) and with -Pargs=200. Compare the times, and explain any surprise.

code.title: LockGranularityDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** The same random transfers under one ledger-wide lock, then under per-account locks taken in id order. */ public class LockGranularityDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 10_000; // guarded by lock (or by the global lock) Account(int id) { this.id = id; } } interface Mover { void move(Account from, Account to, long cents); } static final AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(); // transfers inside a critical section right now static final AtomicInteger mostInside = new AtomicInteger(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int work = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 50; // extra steps inside the lock, per transfer ReentrantLock global = new ReentrantLock(); Mover oneLock = (from, to, cents) -> { global.lock(); // every transfer waits for every other one try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } sign(work); // stands in for real work: an entry, a signature } finally { global.unlock(); } }; Mover perAccount = (from, to, cents) -> { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to; // lower id first: no cycle can form Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock.lock(); try { second.lock.lock(); try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } sign(work); } finally { second.lock.unlock(); } } finally { first.lock.unlock(); } }; System.out.printf("8 threads x 50,000 transfers, %d accounts, %d steps of work inside the lock%n", ACCOUNTS, work); for (int round = 0; round < 3; round++) { // round 0 only warms up the JIT time("one ledger lock ", oneLock, round > 0); time("per-account locks", perAccount, round > 0); } } static void sign(int steps) { int now = inside.incrementAndGet(); mostInside.accumulateAndGet(now, Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); inside.decrementAndGet(); } static void time(String label, Mover mover, boolean print) throws InterruptedException { Account[] accounts = new Account[ACCOUNTS]; for (int i = 0; i < ACCOUNTS; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread w = new Thread(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int n = 0; n < 50_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS), b = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS - 1); if (b >= a) b++; mover.move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)); } }); w.start(); workers.add(w); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); go.countDown(); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long total = 0; for (Account a : accounts) total += a.balance; // after join(): every write is visible if (print) System.out.printf("%s %5d ms, total %,d, most transfers in progress at once: %d%n", label, ms, total, mostInside.get()); mostInside.set(0); } }

to.balance += cents } sign(work) // stands in for real work: an entry, a signature } } val perAccount = { from: GranularityAccount, to: GranularityAccount, cents: Long -> val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // lower id first: no cycle can form val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents } sign(work) } } } println("8 threads x 50,000 transfers, 50 accounts, $work steps of work inside the lock") for (round in 0 until 3) { // round 0 only warms up the JIT time("one ledger lock ", oneLock, round > 0) time("per-account locks", perAccount, round > 0) } } private fun sign(steps: Int) { val now = inside.incrementAndGet() mostInside.accumulateAndGet(now, ::maxOf) repeat(steps) { Thread.onSpinWait() } inside.decrementAndGet() } private fun time(label: String, mover: (GranularityAccount, GranularityAccount, Long) -> Unit, print: Boolean) { val accounts = Array(50) { GranularityAccount(it) } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(8) { thread { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() go.await() repeat(50_000) { val a = rnd.nextInt(50) var b = rnd.nextInt(49) if (b >= a) b++ mover(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)) } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() go.countDown() workers.forEach { it.join() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val total = accounts.sumOf { it.balance } // after join(): every write is visible if (print) println("%s %5d ms, total %,d, most transfers in progress at once: %d".format(label, ms, total, mostInside.get())) mostInside.set(0) }

try.expect: With one lock the last column is always 1. With per-account locks it shows about as many as your cores (4 or 5 on the 4-core machine used here; a thread paused by the OS inside a lock still counts). The times vary with your machine and its load. On the busy machine used here the per-account version was faster in some runs and slower in others, and with -Pargs=0 the single lock often won, because handing a lock from thread to thread costs more than the few instructions it guards. The total is 500,000 in every row: both strategies keep the invariants.

sections.h: A stress harness that tests every invariant
sections.html:
A stress test for the ledger has to make threads collide, then check every invariant. Testing and debugging concurrent code listed the habits: a start line so the threads overlap, more threads than cores, many operations, and checks after join(). The lab's harness runs 8 threads that each make 100,000 random transfers between 50 accounts:

Java
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(threads), go = new CountDownLatch(1);
List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) {
    int me = i;
    workers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
        ready.countDown();
        try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }   // the start line
        long ok = 0, no = 0;                       // counted in locals: nothing shared
        for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) {
            if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++; else no++;
        }
        applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no;        // one slot per thread
    }));
}
ready.await(); go.countDown();                     // release them together...
for (Thread w : workers) w.join();                 // ...and wait for all of them
Kotlin
val ready = CountDownLatch(threads); val go = CountDownLatch(1)
val workers = List(threads) { me ->
    thread {
        ready.countDown()
        go.await()                                 // the start line
        var ok = 0L; var no = 0L                   // counted in locals: nothing shared
        repeat(perThread) { n ->
            if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++ else no++
        }
        applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no         // one slot per thread
    }
}
ready.await(); go.countDown()                      // release them together...
workers.forEach { it.join() }                      // ...and wait for all of them

After the joins, the test checks: the total is still 500,000, no balance is negative, applied plus refused is 800,000 so no transfer vanished, and some transfers were refused, which proves the overdraft branch ran at all.

That list has a hole, and this section's demo falls into it. Take a ledger that locks in id order but checks the balance before it takes the locks. Money is still conserved, because each move is atomic. Balances look fine at the end, because a later credit usually tops up an account that went negative. Yet while it ran, thousands of debits took an account below zero. An end-of-run check sees a healthy ledger.

So check each invariant where it can break, as well as at the end. The lab's Account.debit throws IllegalStateException when a debit would overdraw, so a race that overdraws fails the stress test at once. The check costs one comparison, and in production it turns a silent loss into an error that pages someone. In a database, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint does the same job.

Then remember what a pass means. Eight threads and 800,000 transfers that find nothing make the ledger more believable. They don't prove it. The proof is the argument you can make for each invariant from the code, which is why you wrote the invariants down first.

try.title: Find the bug that conserves money
steps: Read CheckOutsideLockDemo. Both ledgers lock accounts in id order. The first checks the balance, looks up a fee, then takes the locks and moves the money. The second takes the locks, then checks.
Predict which invariants each version breaks, then run it.
Find the line that counts overdrafts. Explain why the "negative at the end" column misses what it counts.

code.title: CheckOutsideLockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Two ledgers that both lock accounts in id order. One checks the balance before it takes the * locks, the other checks after. Run each under 8 threads and test every invariant. */ public class CheckOutsideLockDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final AtomicInteger overdrafts = new AtomicInteger(); // debits that left a balance below zero static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 10_000; // guarded by lock Account(int id) { this.id = id; } long read() { lock.lock(); try { return balance; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } // the bug: the check runs under from's lock, but that lock is released before the move static void checkFirst(Account from, Account to, long cents) { if (from.read() < cents) return; // check lookUpFee(); // a slow step, outside any lock locked(from, to, () -> move(from, to, cents)); // act, later } // the fix: check and act inside the same two locks static void checkInside(Account from, Account to, long cents) { lookUpFee(); // the same slow step, still outside the locks locked(from, to, () -> { if (from.balance >= cents) move(from, to, cents); }); } static void move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; if (from.balance < 0) overdrafts.incrementAndGet(); // the invariant, checked at the moment it can break } // stands in for a call to a fee table; it widens the gap between check and act static void lookUpFee() { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); } static void locked(Account a, Account b, Runnable body) { Account first = a.id < b.id ? a : b, second = first == a ? b : a; first.lock.lock(); try { second.lock.lock(); try { body.run(); } finally { second.lock.unlock(); } } finally { first.lock.unlock(); } } interface Mover { void move(Account from, Account to, long cents); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { runVariant("check, then lock and move", CheckOutsideLockDemo::checkFirst); runVariant("lock, then check and move", CheckOutsideLockDemo::checkInside); } static void runVariant(String label, Mover mover) throws InterruptedException { Account[] accounts = new Account[ACCOUNTS]; for (int i = 0; i < ACCOUNTS; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread w = new Thread(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int n = 0; n < 100_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS), b = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS - 1); if (b >= a) b++; mover.move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)); } }); w.start(); workers.add(w); } go.countDown(); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); long total = 0, negative = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { total += a.balance; if (a.balance < 0) negative++; } System.out.printf("%s%n total %,d %s, negative at the end: %d, overdrafts while running: %,d%n", label, total, total == 500_000 ? "(conserved)" : "(WRONG)", negative, overdrafts.getAndSet(0)); } }

alt.title: CheckOutsideLockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock private class CheckedAccount(val id: Int) { val lock = ReentrantLock() var balance = 10_000L // guarded by lock fun read(): Long = lock.withLock { balance } } private val overdrafts = AtomicInteger() // debits that left a balance below zero // the bug: the check runs under from's lock, but that lock is released before the move private fun checkFirst(from: CheckedAccount, to: CheckedAccount, cents: Long) { if (from.read() < cents) return // check lookUpFee() // a slow step, outside any lock locked(from, to) { move(from, to, cents) } // act, later } // the fix: check and act inside the same two locks private fun checkInside(from: CheckedAccount, to: CheckedAccount, cents: Long) { lookUpFee() // the same slow step, still outside the locks locked(from, to) { if (from.balance >= cents) move(from, to, cents) } } private fun move(from: CheckedAccount, to: CheckedAccount, cents: Long) { from.balance -= cents to.balance += cents if (from.balance < 0) overdrafts.incrementAndGet() // the invariant, checked at the moment it can break } // stands in for a call to a fee table; it widens the gap between check and act private fun lookUpFee() = repeat(200) { Thread.onSpinWait() } private fun locked(a: CheckedAccount, b: CheckedAccount, body: () -> Unit) { val first = if (a.id < b.id) a else b val second = if (first === a) b else a first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { body() } } } /** * Two ledgers that both lock accounts in id order. One checks the balance before it takes the * locks, the other checks after. Run each under 8 threads and test every invariant. */ fun main() { runVariant("check, then lock and move", ::checkFirst) runVariant("lock, then check and move", ::checkInside) } private fun runVariant(label: String, mover: (CheckedAccount, CheckedAccount, Long) -> Unit) { val accounts = Array(50) { CheckedAccount(it) } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(8) { thread { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() go.await() repeat(100_000) { val a = rnd.nextInt(50) var b = rnd.nextInt(49) if (b >= a) b++ mover(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)) } } } go.countDown() workers.forEach { it.join() } val total = accounts.sumOf { it.balance } val negative = accounts.count { it.balance < 0 } println(label) println(" total %,d %s, negative at the end: %d, overdrafts while running: %,d" .format(total, if (total == 500_000L) "(conserved)" else "(WRONG)", negative, overdrafts.getAndSet(0))) }

try.expect: Both totals are 500,000 and neither ledger ends with a negative balance. The first one still overdrew accounts a few thousand times while it ran (3,537 times in one run here); the second never did. Each move was atomic, so invariant 1 held. Invariant 2 broke in the gap between the check and the locks, and later credits hid the evidence before the end.

analogy: Picture a vault room where every safe-deposit box has its own key on a numbered hook. A clerk who moves cash between two boxes must hold both keys while doing it, and the house rule says: take the lower-numbered key first. Two clerks who both need boxes 3 and 7 never end up each holding one key and waiting for the other; one of them waits at hook 3 with empty hands. One key for the whole room would also be correct, and every clerk would queue at the door. The analogy breaks in one place: a real clerk who opens a box and finds it short of cash stops. A thread checks only what your code tells it to check, at the moment you tell it, which is why the check has to sit inside the locks.
world: Your payment services lean on the same invariants, usually through the database: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on two account rows, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint, a unique key on the transfer id. Row locks deadlock exactly like Java locks when two transactions lock the same two rows in opposite orders, and the database then fails one of them with a deadlock error. The fix is the same global order: lock the rows sorted by account id. An in-memory ledger like this one shows up in front of the database: a wallet balance cache, a per-merchant spend limit, the local state of a Temporal workflow. And a Kafka consumer that reuses one mutable DTO per record has the importer's bug the day someone hands records to a pool.
mistake: The most common real mistake is checking the balance in one step and moving the money in another: read the balance (often under the account's lock), decide, then lock both accounts and transfer. Each step is thread-safe, so the code looks careful. It is check-then-act across two critical sections, and another transfer can spend the same money in between. It hides well, because money is still conserved and later credits cover the overdraft before any end-of-day report runs. The fix is to put the check inside the critical section that moves the money, and to guard the invariant where it can break: a debit that would overdraw throws.

compare.title: The ledger's apply in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Ledger.java
java.html: public Outcome apply(Transfer t) { Account from = account(t.from()); Account to = account(t.to()); Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; from.debit(t.cents()); to.credit(t.cents()); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } }

kotlin.title: Ledger.kt
kotlin.html: fun apply(t: Transfer): Outcome { val from = account(t.from) val to = account(t.to) val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from return first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS from.debit(t.cents) to.credit(t.cents) Outcome.APPLIED } } }

compare.note: Kotlin's withLock is an inline function that calls lock(), runs the block and calls unlock() in a finally, so the two nested try/finally blocks become two nested lambdas. Because it is inline, return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS inside the block returns from apply itself, and the locks are still released. from.id < to.id on strings calls the same compareTo as the Java version. The immutable Transfer differs only in style: a Kotlin data class of vals is exactly as shallow as a Java record. Both make the fields final, and neither copies a mutable list you pass in.

worked.title: Add a fee without breaking the invariants

steps.say: The product team wants a fee on each transfer, paid into a fee account. Money is still conserved: the sender pays cents + fee, the receiver gets cents and the fee account gets fee. Three accounts now change in one step. Here is the first attempt. Read it against the three invariants and the lock order before you go on.
steps.code: Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); from.lock().lock(); to.lock().lock(); feeAccount.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; from.debit(t.cents() + fee); to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { feeAccount.lock().unlock(); to.lock().unlock(); from.lock().unlock(); } }

alt.html: fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) from.lock.lock() to.lock.lock() feeAccount.lock.lock() try { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS from.debit(t.cents + fee) to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { feeAccount.lock.unlock() to.lock.unlock() from.lock.unlock() } }

steps.say: Two bugs. The locks are ordered by role, not by id: a transfer from acc-02 to acc-05 locks 02 then 05, while a transfer from acc-05 to acc-02 locks 05 then 02. That is the deadlock cycle again. And the check tests cents, but the debit takes cents + fee, so a sender with exactly cents left goes below zero. The lab's debit would throw; a plain field would quietly go negative.

Sort every account the operation touches by id, lock them in that order, and release them in reverse. The same code works for two accounts, three, or a payroll batch of fifty. distinct() covers the case where the sender is the fee account itself, because a ReentrantLock taken twice must also be released twice.
steps.code: Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); List<Account> touched = Stream.of(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Account::id)) // 1. one global order, any number of locks .toList(); touched.forEach(a -> a.lock().lock()); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents() + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents() + fee); // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { for (int i = touched.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) touched.get(i).lock().unlock(); // 4. reverse order } }

alt.html: fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) val touched = listOf(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sortedBy { it.id } // 1. one global order, any number of locks touched.forEach { it.lock.lock() } try { if (from.balance < t.cents + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents + fee) // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { touched.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } // 4. reverse order } }

steps.say: Check it against the invariants. Conservation: the sender loses cents + fee and the other two gain exactly that. No overdraft: the check and the debit use the same amount under the same locks. Whole or nothing: all three changes happen inside one set of locks. No deadlock: plain apply locks two accounts in id order and this method locks three in id order, so any two operations agree on which lock comes first. Where the fee account's id sorts among the customer ids doesn't matter. Only the rule matters.

lab.title: Build the ledger and the harness that tries to break it
steps: Run the tests once. All nine fail. Read Account: you don't change it, but its debit and credit throw unless you hold that account's lock, and debit throws on an overdraft.
In Transfer, add a compact constructor: Objects.requireNonNull for id, from and to, and an IllegalArgumentException when cents <= 0 or from.equals(to).

Write Ledger.apply: look up both accounts, pick first and second with id().compareTo, lock them in that order with nested try/finally, then check the balance and move the money while you hold both locks.

Write StressHarness.run: a ready latch and a go latch, threads workers that each make perThread random transfers with ThreadLocalRandom, per-thread counts stored in a long[] slot at the end, then join every worker and add up the slots.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then break apply on purpose: lock from first and to second, and watch the deadlock test fail after its 15 second limit. Put the order back.
hints: Two different random accounts without a retry loop: int a = rnd.nextInt(n); int b = rnd.nextInt(n - 1); if (b >= a) b++;.
Build each transfer's id from the thread number and the loop counter, such as "t" + me + "-" + n. The test checks that no id repeats.
Call ThreadLocalRandom.current() inside the worker's lambda, not before it. Each thread needs its own generator.
If the overlap test fails, check that each worker counts down ready before it waits on go, and that run waits on ready before it counts down go.
lab.done: All nine tests in LedgerTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the ordered two-lock transfer from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write Outcome move(Account from, Account to, long cents) for accounts that have a unique id() and a ReentrantLock lock(). It must never deadlock, never overdraw and always release both locks. Then compare with the answer. Is your balance check inside both locks?

answer.html: Outcome move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to; // lower id first, always Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // check under both locks from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } }

alt.html: fun move(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long): Outcome { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // lower id first, always val second = if (first === from) to else from return first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance < cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // check under both locks from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) Outcome.APPLIED } } }

recap: Write the invariants first: money is conserved, no balance goes below zero, a transfer is whole or not at all. Every line of apply protects one of them.
Debit and credit happen in one critical section that holds both accounts' locks, and the balance check sits inside it too. Anything else is check-then-act.
Lock accounts in one global order by a unique, stable id (compareTo, never hashCode). For more than two accounts, sort them all, lock in order, release in reverse.
A transfer is an immutable value checked in its constructor: safe to hand to any thread, and never invalid. A reused mutable row handed to a pool delivers the wrong data.
A stress harness needs a start line, more threads than cores, many operations, and checks of every invariant, both at the end and where each one can break.
Per-account locks let transfers on different accounts run at once. With little work inside the lock one lock can be as fast, so count and measure before you argue.

explain.prompt: A reviewer looks at your apply and says: "Why two locks and all this ordering? Put synchronized on the method and be done." Explain what that would give you, what it would cost, and why the balance check sits where it does.
explain.answer: synchronized on apply locks the whole ledger, so every transfer waits for every other one. It is correct: it protects all three invariants, and with one lock there is no order to get wrong. The cost is parallelism. A transfer between two accounts nobody else touches still waits in line, and at most one transfer is ever in progress. With per-account locks, transfers on different accounts run at the same time, at the price of a rule everyone must follow: lock the lower id first, or two opposite transfers can deadlock. Whether that parallelism buys speed depends on the work inside the lock and on the cores you have, so I'd measure it. On JDK 21 I'd also avoid synchronized for code that virtual threads will call. Wherever the locks are, the balance check stays inside them: a check before them is check-then-act, and another transfer could spend the money between the check and the debit.

deeper.html:
Two directions this design grows in real systems.

The first is hot accounts. A merchant settlement account that receives a third of all transfers serializes them on its one lock, whatever the order. A common fix is to split it into a few sub-accounts, each with its own lock, credit a random one, and add them up for the balance. For a single account you could also drop the lock and use a compare-and-set loop, as Atomics and compare-and-set showed. The check becomes part of the loop:

Java
boolean debit(AtomicLong balance, long cents) {
    while (true) {
        long current = balance.get();
        if (current < cents) return false;                   // the check is inside the loop
        if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true;
    }
}
Kotlin
fun debit(balance: AtomicLong, cents: Long): Boolean {
    while (true) {
        val current = balance.get()
        if (current < cents) return false                    // the check is inside the loop
        if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true
    }
}

That is lock-free for one account. A transfer touches two, and two compare-and-sets in a row are not one atomic step: between them the money is in neither account, which breaks invariant 3. That is why locks are the simpler tool for transfers.

The second is the database. A persisted ledger uses the same ideas with other tools: row locks taken in account id order, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint, and a unique key on the transfer id so a retried request applies once. Many ledgers never update a balance in place at all. They append immutable entries, one debit and one credit per transfer, and compute balances from them. That is double-entry bookkeeping, and invariant 1 becomes "the entries of every transfer sum to zero", which you can check one transfer at a time.
